terms.meaning: how exact a date is: a day, a month, a season, a year, or unknown.
a word such as 'TBC' that stands in for a date that is not known yet.
the standard way of writing a date as year, month, day, such as 2016-03-31.

sections.name: File setup, DatePrecision
sections.title: Rule set, precision types and header rules
sections.what: Explains the fixed and editable rules in the header and defines the rule set name and the list of precision levels.
sections.why: The rule set name is a version tag so stored results can be matched to the rules that made them.
sections.watch_out: Changing the rule set name makes every rule-based date look changed on the next convention edit.

sections.name: ResolvedDate
sections.title: The resolved date record
sections.what: Defines the shape of one resolved date: the stated text, precision, resolved day or null, the rule in words, and the convention used.
sections.why: Keeps the original wording next to the answer so a reader can check the reasoning.
sections.watch_out: The resolved day is null when refused, so every caller must handle that case.

sections.name: DateConventionDef
sections.title: The convention record
sections.what: Defines the shape of one convention: key, group, label, definition, span months, calculation month, refused flag and sort order.
sections.why: Lets conventions be stored as data and edited without changing code.
sections.watch_out: A null calculation month means refused, and that is the only switch for refusal.

sections.name: conv
sections.title: Helper for writing conventions
sections.what: Short helper that builds one convention entry and sets the refused flag automatically when there is no calculation month.
sections.why: Keeps the default list short to write.
sections.watch_out: Arguments are positional, so swapping two month numbers silently changes a convention.

sections.name: DEFAULT_DATE_CONVENTIONS, ACTIVE
sections.title: Built-in conventions and active list
sections.what: Holds the built-in conventions such as early, mid, late, year, quarters, halves and seasons, plus the winter convention that is refused because it crosses two calendar years. It also holds the active working copy used by the resolver.
sections.why: Likely reason: the app needs a working set of conventions before the database has any rows.
sections.watch_out: The winter convention is refused by design, so any wording that uses it will never resolve.

sections.name: setDateConventions
sections.title: Replacing the active conventions
sections.what: Replaces the active list with stored values. Unknown keys are ignored, and any convention without a calculation month is always refused.
sections.why: Lets stored edits take effect without a restart.
sections.watch_out: A key that is not in the built-in list is silently ignored, so a new convention cannot be added by data alone.

sections.name: getDateConventions
sections.title: Reading the active conventions
sections.what: Returns the active conventions sorted by their sort order.
sections.why: Likely reason: the conventions page and the rest of the app need a sorted list. Not confirmed in the packet.

sections.name: MONTHS, MONTH_ABBR
sections.title: Month names and spellings
sections.what: Maps month names in many spellings, including full names and short forms such as sept, to month numbers, and holds the short names used in displays.
sections.why: Real sources write months in many ways, so one lookup covers them.
sections.watch_out: A spelling missing from this list is not recognised, so check here first when a month fails to resolve.

sections.name: lastDay
sections.title: Last day of a month
sections.what: Returns the last day of a given month as a YYYY-MM-DD text value, handling leap years through the calendar.
sections.why: Named months resolve to their last day, so the app needs this value.

sections.name: refuse, MONTH_RANGE
sections.title: Refusal helper and month range text
sections.what: Builds a refused result with no day and a reason. Also builds short text for a span such as Jan to Mar for display.
sections.why: Keeps refusals consistent and gives readable rule text.
sections.watch_out: The span text is empty when either month is missing, which then appears blank in the rule text.

sections.name: byConvention
sections.title: Resolving through a convention
sections.what: Looks up a convention and returns a refused result if it is refused, otherwise the last day of its calculation month in the given year, with rule text that states the span and the day used.
sections.why: Keeps the explanation of each resolved date readable.
sections.watch_out: An unknown convention key is not handled, so the lookup fails instead of refusing cleanly.

sections.name: resolveStatedDate (part 1)
sections.title: Tidying the stated date
sections.what: Main entry point. Turns raw text into a clean form: returns nothing for blank text or placeholders, then lower-cases it, removes approximate words such as 'around', removes approximate symbols, and drops bracketed notes. The matching step continues in the next section.
sections.why: Likely reason: real source text is messy, so tidying first lets one set of rules match many spellings. The comment says it never guesses.
sections.watch_out: Removing words such as 'by' and 'planned' means a phrase such as 'planned by 2030' is read the same as '2030'.

sections.name: resolveStatedDate: if
sections.title: Reading quarters, halves, seasons and parts of a year
sections.what: The second half of the same reading. It recognises Q1 to Q4, first to fourth quarter, H1 or 2H, seasons (fall counts as autumn), early, mid, late or end, and bare years, and sends each to the convention path.
sections.why: Likely reason: these are the common ways a date is written, and each maps to a named convention.
sections.watch_out: The early, mid, late and end pattern is loose, so unusual wording could match a convention it should not.

sections.name: monthsBetween
sections.title: Whole months between two dates
sections.what: Counts the whole months from one year and month to another, ignoring the day.
sections.why: Likely reason: schedule slippage is measured in months.
sections.watch_out: Partial months are dropped, so a date only a few days off can show as a whole month different.

summary: Decides which exact calendar day the app uses for each date written in a source, keeps the wording as stated, and records how the day was reached.
purpose: Makes dates comparable across sources. Exact days stay as they are, named months resolve to their last day, and fuzzy wording resolves through editable conventions. Anything it cannot resolve is kept as text with no day.
why: The file header says the code never guesses. Refused forms (ranges, two dates in one phrase, no year) keep their text and produce no day, so a reader sees the original wording.
how: 1. Tidy the raw text: squash spaces, lower-case it, drop words such as 'around' or 'by', and drop anything in brackets. 2. Return nothing for blank text or placeholders such as 'TBC' or 'not disclosed'. 3. Check the cleaned text against the fixed rules. The rest of the matching logic, lines 120 to 191, was not in the packet.
inputs: One raw date string from a source, or nothing. The active convention list held in memory.
outputs: A resolved date record with the stated text, precision level, the resolved day or null, the rule in words, and the convention key used. Returns nothing for blank or placeholder text.
risks: A wrong day changes every calculation that uses it. The active convention list is shared in memory, so an edit affects all callers at once. Removing words such as 'by' or 'planned' can make a target date read the same as a plain year.
debug: Pass the suspect string through the resolver and read the rule text. A null result with 'not resolved' in the rule text names the reason. Check the convention key shown. If a date changed unexpectedly, check the rule set name and the convention table.
